1→# Code Review: Polygon Rendering Glitches (2026-02-10)
     2→
     3→Thorough review of `src/another_world_vm.asm` against the reference C++ implementation
     4→([Fabien Sanglard's AW-VM](https://github.com/fabiensanglard/Another-World-Bytecode-Interpreter/blob/master/src/video.cpp)).
     5→
     6→## Bug #1: `drawPoint` clobbers x coordinate (DEFINITE BUG)
     7→
     8→**Location:** `drawPoint` lines 184-196
     9→
    10→**Problem:** `LD DE, 320` overwrites DE, which held the x coordinate. Then `EXTZ XDE`
    11→zero-extends 320 (not x), and `ADD XWA, XDE` computes `y*320 + 320` instead of `y*320 + x`.
    12→
    13→Every single-pixel point is drawn at the wrong x position.
    14→
    15→**Fix:** Save DE (x) before loading 320 into DE for multiply, restore after.
    16→
    17→## Bug #2: Opcode 0x40 zoom case 3 — video2 not selected (WRONG POLYGONS)
    18→
    19→**Location:** `_0x40_zoom_case3` (line ~1391) and `readAndDrawPolygonHierarchy` (line ~863)
    20→
    21→**Problem:** The reference sets `m_useSegVideo2 = true` for zoom case 3, using video2 as the
    22→polygon data source. Our code always uses `INTRO_VIDEO_1`. The `INTRO_VIDEO_2` data IS
    23→available (bincluded), just never referenced.
    24→
    25→Both places that resolve polygon data pointers are affected:
    26→- Opcode 0x40 handler: `LD XIX, INTRO_VIDEO_1`
    27→- Hierarchy function: `ADD XIX, INTRO_VIDEO_1`
    28→
    29→**Fix:** Add a `CUR_VIDEO_DATA` variable (DD), default to `INTRO_VIDEO_1`, set to
    30→`INTRO_VIDEO_2` in zoom case 3. Reference it in both the 0x40 handler and hierarchy.
    31→Reset back to VIDEO_1 after the opcode completes.
    32→
    33→## Bug #3: `readVertices` uses signed shift on unsigned product (LATENT)
    34→
    35→**Location:** `readVertices` and `readAndDrawPolygonHierarchy` — all `SRAW 6, WA` occurrences
    36→
    37→**Problem:** `SRAW 6, WA` performs a signed arithmetic shift right. The product `byte * zoom`
    38→is unsigned (0 to 65025). When the product exceeds 32767 (bit 15 set), SRAW sign-extends,
    39→giving a wrong negative result.
    40→
    41→**Impact:** Only manifests when `byte * zoom > 32767`, i.e., zoom > 128 with large vertex
    42→bytes. For the default zoom 0x40 (64), max product is 255 * 64 = 16320, well under 32767.
    43→**Harmless for the intro** but would be wrong for later game parts with non-default zoom.

1→# CLAUDE.md
     2→
     3→This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
     4→
     5→## Project Overview
     6→
     7→Custom ROM development for the **Technics KN5000** arranger keyboard. ROMs can be tested in MAME's kn5000 driver and potentially installed on real hardware.
     8→
     9→**Target Hardware:**
    10→- CPU: Toshiba TMP94C241F (TLCS-900/H2), 25 MHz, 32-bit CISC
    11→- Display: MN89304 VGA-compatible LCD controller, 320x240 @ 8bpp
    12→- Serial: SC0 for MIDI/Computer Interface, SC1 for Control Panel
    13→- Memory: 2MB Program ROM at 0xE00000-0xFFFFFF, 512KB VRAM at 0x1A0000
    14→
    15→## Build Commands
    16→
    17→```bash
    18→make          # Build maincpu ROM and create MAME ROM set (default)
    19→make maincpu  # Build as standalone main CPU ROM (2MB, for MAME testing)
    20→make extension# Build as HDAE5000 extension board ROM (512KB)
    21→make build    # Build custom ROM only (out/custom_program.rom)
    22→make romset   # Create complete MAME ROM set
    23→make test     # Run in MAME emulator
    24→make clean    # Remove build artifacts (preserves ROM set)
    25→make distclean# Remove everything including ROM set
    26→make check    # Verify tools and original ROMs are available
    27→```
    28→
    29→**Dual-target build:** Uses `ifdef TARGET_MAINCPU` / `ifdef TARGET_EXTENSION` conditional assembly in `src/main.asm`. The VM code in `src/another_world_vm.asm` is shared between both targets.
    30→
    31→**Requirements:**
    32→- ASL Macro Assembler at `../../tools/asl/asl`
    33→- Original KN5000 ROMs at `/mnt/shared/kn5000_original_roms/kn5000/`
    34→- Game resources in `src/resources/` and `src/` (see README for extraction)
    35→
    36→**Output:**
    37→- Build artifacts: `out/`
    38→- MAME ROM set: `/mnt/shared/custom_kn5000_roms/anotherworld/kn5000/`
    39→
    40→## Architecture
    41→
    42→**Maincpu target** initializes at reset vector 0xFFFEE0, then:
    43→1. Disables watchdog, sets up stack
    44→2. Configures memory controller and DRAM
    45→3. Initializes VGA display (320x240, 8bpp palette mode)
    46→4. Jumps to VM ENTRY point
    47→
    48→**Extension target** is loaded by the KN5000 firmware via the XAPR header and jumps directly to the VM ENTRY point.
    49→
    50→**Memory layout differs by target:**
    51→- **Maincpu:** RAM at 0x010000, page buffers at 0x020000-0x050000, offscreen at 0x060000 (in 1MB DRAM)
    52→- **Extension:** RAM at 0x200000, page buffers at 0x240000-0x270000 (in 512KB extension SRAM)
    53→
    54→**Key source files:**
    55→- `src/main.asm` - Unified platform wrapper (conditional assembly for maincpu/extension)
    56→- `src/another_world_vm.asm` - Another World bytecode VM (shared between targets)
    57→- `src/includes/local_macros.inc` - TLCS-900 instruction macros for ASL
    58→
    59→## Reference Repositories (Read-Only)
    60→
    61→These sibling repositories contain essential reference material. **Do not modify them; all changes go in this repo only.**
    62→
    63→### Hardware Documentation: `../../kn5000-docs/`
    64→| Topic | File | Key Information |
    65→|-------|------|-----------------|
    66→| Memory Map | `memory-map.md` | ROM/RAM addresses, VRAM at 0x1A0000, VGA at 0x170000 |

    91→
    92→**ASL quirks for TMP94C241:**
    93→- Use `cpu 96c141` directive
    94→- Some instructions need macros (see `macros.inc`): `LDIR_94`, `LDA_XWA_IMM24`, `CALR`

   101→ld (XDE), A           ; Register indirect
   102→LDA_XWA_IMM24 addr    ; Load 24-bit address into XWA
   103→```
   104→
   105→## Hardware Quick Reference
   106→
   107→**VGA Display:**
   108→- Base: 0x170000 (+ VGA port offset, e.g., 0x1703C8 for DAC)
   109→- VRAM: 0x1A0000, linear framebuffer, 1 byte per pixel
   110→- Palette: 6-bit RGB values via DAC registers
   111→
   112→**Serial Port SC0:**
   113→- SC0BUF (0xD0): Data buffer
   114→- SC0CR (0xD1): Control (bit 1 = TX empty)
   115→- SC0MOD (0xD2): Mode (0x29 = 8N1 with baud gen)

   120→2. Configure memory controller (MSAR/MAMR registers)
   121→3. Initialize DRAM with timing delays
   122→4. Set stack pointer to internal RAM
   123→
   124→## Another World VM Architecture
   125→
   126→The VM interprets big-endian bytecode (Amiga/68k origin) on a little-endian TLCS-900 CPU.
   127→
   128→**Bytecode execution:**
   129→- `XIX` register points to current bytecode position during instruction execution
   130→- `_end_of_EXECUTE_INSTRUCTION` recomputes `VM_PC` from `XIX` offset — XIX must point to bytecode
   131→- `_after_PC_update` skips VM_PC recomputation — use when VM_PC was already set (JMP, CALL, RET, NEXT_THREAD)
   132→- Opcodes that replace XIX with non-bytecode pointers (0x80, 0x40 video) must save VM_PC BEFORE the replacement and use `_after_PC_update`
   133→
   134→**Thread model:**
   135→- 64 threads, each with a PC slot in `THREADS_DATA` and activation state in `VM_IS_CHANNEL_ACTIVE`
   136→- `pauseThread` saves requested_PC; `NEXT_THREAD` scans for next active thread
   137→- `CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS` commits requested_PC → PC at frame boundaries
   138→- `INACTIVE_THREAD` (0xFFFE) marks unused thread slots
   139→
   140→**Video pages:**
   141→- 4 page buffers (320x240 @ 8bpp = 76,800 bytes each)
   142→- Page IDs: 0-3 map directly; 0xFF = current back buffer; 0xFE = current front buffer
   143→- `GET_PAGE_PTR` resolves page ID → 24-bit address
   144→
   145→**Endianness:** All `fetch_word()` operations must byte-swap with `EX W, A` after reading via `LD WA, (XIX)`.
   146→
   147→**Helper functions:**
   148→- `_read_vm_var`: Input A=index, Output DE=value (clobbers XIY/XWA)
   149→- `_write_vm_var`: Input A=index, DE=value (clobbers XIY/XWA)

   156→- Video polygons: `src/resources/resource-0x19.bin` (video1), `resource-0x1a.bin` (video2)
   157→- Screen bitmaps: `src/resources/resource-0x49.bin`, `resource-0x53.bin`

   159→## TLCS-900 Pitfalls (Learned from Debugging)
   160→
   161→**INC instruction encoding:** Only supports values 1, 2, 4, 8 (encoded in 2-bit field). ASL assembler silently accepts any value but encodes raw bits. MAME treats the 3-bit field literally (`value ? value : 8`), so `INC 3` "works" in MAME but is **undefined on real TMP94C241F**. Always use `ADD` for non-power-of-2 increments.
   162→
   163→**Register clobbering:**
   164→- `LD BC, WA` clobbers B — save B to stack first if needed later
   165→- `POP WA` restores both W and A — don't follow with `LD A, W` (overwrites restored A)
   166→- `LDIRW` uses XHL=src, XDE=dst, XBC=word_count (not XIX/XIY)
   167→
   168→**Signed vs unsigned shifts:** `SRA` (arithmetic shift right) sign-extends; `SRL` (logical shift right) zero-fills. Use `SRL` for unsigned nibble extraction (e.g., extracting high nibble of a byte).
   169→
   170→**AW palette → VGA DAC conversion:**
   171→- AW format: 2 bytes/color, `0x0RGB`. Byte 0 low nibble = R, byte 1 high nibble = G, byte 1 low nibble = B
   172→- VGA DAC expects 6-bit values (0-63) in R, G, B order; AW uses 4-bit (0-15)
   173→- Must `SLA 2, A` to scale each channel from 4-bit to 6-bit

Now let me create a comprehensive summary by gathering the specific timing code sections:

Based on my thorough search of the codebase, here is a complete analysis of the timing-related code in the Another World VM port:

## TIMING ANALYSIS: Another World VM on KN5000

### 1. **FRAME TIMING MECHANISM**

The frame timing is currently implemented using **busy-wait delay loops** rather than hardware timers:

**Location:** `src/another_world_vm.asm`, lines 383-399

```asm
LONG_PAUSE:
	LD BC, 0
LONG_PAUSE_LOOP1:
	LD DE, 080h
LONG_PAUSE_LOOP2:
	DJNZ DE, LONG_PAUSE_LOOP2
	DJNZ BC, LONG_PAUSE_LOOP1
	RET

PAUSE:
	LD BC, 0
PAUSE_LOOP1:
	LD DE, 01h
PAUSE_LOOP2:
	DJNZ DE, PAUSE_LOOP2
	DJNZ BC, PAUSE_LOOP1
	RET
```

**Key findings:**
- `PAUSE` uses nested DJNZ loops with minimal iteration (DE=0x01, BC=0)
- `LONG_PAUSE` uses larger iteration count (DE=0x80)
- **NO hardware timer setup** - These are pure CPU-busy delays
- At 25 MHz (the CPU clock), the exact frame rate depends on instruction cycle counts
- No VSYNC synchronization to hardware

### 2. **EXECUTE_INSTRUCTION LOOP**

**Location:** `src/another_world_vm.asm`, lines 1232-2206

The main execution loop runs **one instruction per iteration**:

```asm
MAIN_LOOP:
	CALL EXECUTE_INSTRUCTION
	JP MAIN_LOOP
```

Each `EXECUTE_INSTRUCTION` call:
1. Fetches one bytecode opcode
2. Executes the operation
3. Updates VM_PC
4. Returns

**Instructions per frame:**
- Executed continuously until `NEXT_THREAD` detects end-of-frame (after all 64 threads)
- No fixed instruction budget - depends on thread scheduling and opcodes executed

### 3. **PAUSETHREAD / NEXT_THREAD / CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS FLOW**

**Frame boundary detection:** `src/another_world_vm.asm`, lines 1185-1229

```asm
NEXT_THREAD:
	CALL INPUT_UPDATE_PLAYER

	LD WA, 0
	LD A, (CURRENT_THREAD)

_next_thread__do_loop:
	INC A
	CP A, 64
	JP NE, _not_end_of_frame
	; == END OF FRAME ==
	LDB (CURRENT_THREAD), 0
	CALL CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS
	LD A, 0FEh
	CALL UPDATE_DISPLAY
	LD A, 0
_not_end_of_frame:
	; ... thread selection logic ...
	LD (VM_PC), DE
	RET
```

**Frame execution model:**
- 64 threads are scanned sequentially
- When thread counter reaches 64 (end of 64-thread cycle), the frame ends
- At frame boundary:
  1. `CURRENT_THREAD` reset to 0
  2. `CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS` called (processes thread state/PC changes)
  3. `UPDATE_DISPLAY` called with page ID 0xFE (swap display buffers)

**PAUSETHREAD instruction (0x06):** `src/another_world_vm.asm`, lines 1563-1585

```asm
; ====  PAUSE_THREAD instruction  ====
CP A, 6
JP NE, INSTRUCTION_IS_NOT_PAUSE_THREAD
LD WA, 0
LD A, (CURRENT_THREAD)
SLA 2, WA
EXTZ XWA
ADD XWA, THREADS_DATA

LD DE, (XWA + REQUESTED_PC_OFFSET)
CP DE, NO_REQUEST
JP NE, _pausethread_after_setting_request
; When there's no other program counter request set
; for this thread, we set the address of the
; next instruction to resume execution
; in the next VM frame.
LD XDE, XIX
SUB XDE, INTRO_BYTECODE
LD (XWA + REQUESTED_PC_OFFSET), DE
_pausethread_after_setting_request:
CALL NEXT_THREAD
JP _after_PC_update
```

### 4. **BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER TIMING (0x10)**

**Location:** `src/another_world_vm.asm`, lines 1967-1991

```asm
; ====  BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER instruction  ====
CP A, 10h
JP NE, INSTRUCTION_IS_NOT_BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER
LD A, (XIX)		; byte pageId
INC XIX

; ... page ID handling ...

POP WA			; restore pageId (A = pageId)
CALL UPDATE_DISPLAY
CALL PAUSE			; Frame timing delay
JP _end_of_EXECUTE_INSTRUCTION
```

**Key point:** `BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER` calls `PAUSE` to add a frame delay after display update.

### 5. **UPDATE_DISPLAY MECHANISM**

**Location:** `src/another_world_vm.asm`, lines 230-254

## TMP94C241F Hardware Timer Information

I've searched the reference documentation and disassembly for complete timer information. Here's what I found:

### Timer Architecture

The TMP94C241F includes **8 timers total**:
- **4x 8-bit timers** (T0, T1, T2, T3)
- **4x 16-bit timers** (T4, T5, T6, T7, T8, T9, TA, TB)

### Register Addresses (SFR = Special Function Registers)

**8-bit Timers (T0-T3):**
```
T01MOD     = 0x84  ; Timer 0/1 Mode Control
T23MOD     = 0x85  ; Timer 2/3 Mode Control
T02FFCR    = 0x82  ; Timer 0/2 Flip-Flop Control
T01FFCR    = 0x81  ; Timer 0/1 Flip-Flop Control
T23FFCR    = 0x89  ; Timer 2/3 Flip-Flop Control
T8RUN      = 0x80  ; 8-bit Timer Run Control Register
TREG0      = 0x88  ; Timer 0 Data Register
TREG1      = 0x89  ; Timer 1 Data Register
TREG2      = 0x8A  ; Timer 2 Data Register
TREG3      = 0x8B  ; Timer 3 Data Register
TRDC       = 0x81  ; Timer Register Double-buffer Control
```

**16-bit Timers (T4-TB):**
```
T4MOD      = 0x98  ; Timer 4 Mode
T4FFCR     = 0x99  ; Timer 4 Flip-Flop Control
T16RUN     = 0x9E  ; 16-bit Timer Run Control
T16CR      = 0x9F  ; 16-bit Timer Control

T6MOD      = 0xA8  ; Timer 6 Mode
T6FFCR     = 0xA9  ; Timer 6 Flip-Flop Control

T8MOD      = 0xB8  ; Timer 8 Mode
T8FFCR     = 0xB9  ; Timer 8 Flip-Flop Control

TAMOD      = 0xC8  ; Timer A Mode
TAFFCR     = 0xC9  ; Timer A Flip-Flop Control

16-bit timer registers (low/high bytes):
TREG4L     = 0x90  ; Timer 4 Low
TREG4H     = 0x91  ; Timer 4 High
TREG5L     = 0x92  ; Timer 5 Low
TREG5H     = 0x93  ; Timer 5 High
TREG6L     = 0xA0  ; Timer 6 Low
TREG6H     = 0xA1  ; Timer 6 High
TREG7L     = 0xA2  ; Timer 7 Low
TREG7H     = 0xA3  ; Timer 7 High
TREG8L     = 0xB0  ; Timer 8 Low
TREG8H     = 0xB1  ; Timer 8 High
TREG9L     = 0xB2  ; Timer 9 Low
TREG9H     = 0xB3  ; Timer 9 High
TREGAL     = 0xC0  ; Timer A Low
TREGAH     = 0xC1  ; Timer A High
TREGBL     = 0xC2  ; Timer B Low
TREGBH     = 0xC3  ; Timer B High

Capture registers:
CAP4L      = 0x94  ; Timer 4 Capture Low
CAP4H      = 0x95  ; Timer 4 Capture High
CAP5L      = 0x96  ; Timer 5 Capture Low
CAP5H      = 0x97  ; Timer 5 Capture High
(Similar pattern for T6-TA)
```

### Clock Configuration

```
CLKMOD = 0x010A  ; Clock Mode Register
```

**Initialization value used:** `0x04` (sets clock mode for peripherals)

### How the Original KN5000 Firmware Uses Timers

**Boot Sequence (shared/boot_hw_init.asm:66-82):**

```asm
; === 8-bit Timer Setup ===
LD (T01MOD), 01dh    ; Timer 0/1 mode = 0x1D
LD (T23MOD), 01dh    ; Timer 2/3 mode = 0x1D
LD (T02FFCR), 000h   ; Flip-flop control = 0
LD (TREG0), 00ah     ; Timer 0 preset = 0x0A
LD (TREG1), 010h     ; Timer 1 preset = 0x10
LD (TRDC), 000h      ; Double-buffer control = 0
SET 1, (T8RUN)       ; Start timers (bit 1 set)

; === 16-bit Timer 4/5 Setup ===
LD (T4MOD), 005h     ; Timer 4 mode = 0x05
LD (T4FFCR), 000h    ; Flip-flop control = 0
LD (T16CR), 000h     ; 16-bit control = 0
db 0Ah, 90h, 01h, 00h       ; TREG4L = 0x0001
db 0Ah, 92h, 09h, 3dh       ; TREG5L = 0x3D09
SET 7, (T16RUN)      ; Bit 7 = prescaler run
SET 0, (T16RUN)      ; Bit 0 = timer run
```

**Sub CPU Usage (kn5000_subprogram_v142.asm:9330-9334):**

Similar 16-bit timer initialization:
```asm
LD (T4MOD), 005h
LD (T4FFCR), 000h
LD (T16CR), 000h
LD (T16RUN), 000h
SET 7, (T16RUN)      ; prescaler: run
```

### Timer Control Bits (T16RUN Register)

- **Bit 0:** Start/stop Timer 4 (0=stop, 1=run)
- **Bit 7:** Start/stop prescaler (0=stop, 1=run)

Both must be set to enable 16-bit timers.

### Key Configuration (T4MOD = 0x05)

The value `0x05` for T4MOD appears to configure:
- Timer mode (counter vs. timer)
- Clock source selection
- Edge/level trigger mode

### Timer Registers for Measuring Elapsed Time

For **16-bit timers** (best for measuring elapsed time):
- Load initial value into TREG4L (low byte) and TREG4H (high byte)
- Enable with `SET 7, (T16RUN)` and `SET 0, (T16RUN)`
- Read current value from TREG4L:TREG4H (16-bit counter)
- Timer counts up/down based on mode

**Note:** The 16-bit registers require special encoding in ASL assembler:
```asm
db 0Ah, 90h, 01h, 00h  ; LDW (TREG4L:24), 0x0001  (ASL unsupported)
```

### Source Files with Timer Information

1. **Register definitions:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/shared/sfr_tmp94c241.asm` (lines 65-125)
2. **Boot initialization:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/shared/boot_hw_init.asm` (lines 66-82)
3. **Sub CPU boot:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/subcpu/boot/kn5000_subcpu_boot.asm` (lines 99-131, 263-317)
4. **Sub CPU program:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/subcpu/kn5000_subprogram_v142.asm` (lines 9330-9334)
5. **Documentation:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-docs/reverse-engineering.md` (lines 840-932)

### Recommended Timer for Elapsed Time Measurement

**Use 16-bit Timer 4 (T4)** because:
1. Already initialized in boot sequence with known configuration
2. 16-bit resolution (up to 65535 counts)
3. Register addresses are well-documented
4. Can be read at any time without stopping the timer
5. Doesn't interfere with other timers (T0-T3 handle different functions)

**Boot Sequence (shared/boot_hw_init.asm:66-82):**

```asm
; === 8-bit Timer Setup ===
LD (T01MOD), 01dh    ; Timer 0/1 mode = 0x1D
LD (T23MOD), 01dh    ; Timer 2/3 mode = 0x1D
LD (T02FFCR), 000h   ; Flip-flop control = 0
LD (TREG0), 00ah     ; Timer 0 preset = 0x0A
LD (TREG1), 010h     ; Timer 1 preset = 0x10
LD (TRDC), 000h      ; Double-buffer control = 0
SET 1, (T8RUN)       ; Start timers (bit 1 set)

; === 16-bit Timer 4/5 Setup ===
LD (T4MOD), 005h     ; Timer 4 mode = 0x05
LD (T4FFCR), 000h    ; Flip-flop control = 0
LD (T16CR), 000h     ; 16-bit control = 0
db 0Ah, 90h, 01h, 00h       ; TREG4L = 0x0001
db 0Ah, 92h, 09h, 3dh       ; TREG5L = 0x3D09
SET 7, (T16RUN)      ; Bit 7 = prescaler run
SET 0, (T16RUN)      ; Bit 0 = timer run
```

**Sub CPU Usage (kn5000_subprogram_v142.asm:9330-9334):**

Similar 16-bit timer initialization:
```asm
LD (T4MOD), 005h
LD (T4FFCR), 000h
LD (T16CR), 000h
LD (T16RUN), 000h
SET 7, (T16RUN)      ; prescaler: run
```

### Timer Control Bits (T16RUN Register)

- **Bit 0:** Start/stop Timer 4 (0=stop, 1=run)
- **Bit 7:** Start/stop prescaler (0=stop, 1=run)

Both must be set to enable 16-bit timers.

### Key Configuration (T4MOD = 0x05)

The value `0x05` for T4MOD appears to configure:
- Timer mode (counter vs. timer)
- Clock source selection
- Edge/level trigger mode

### Timer Registers for Measuring Elapsed Time

For **16-bit timers** (best for measuring elapsed time):
- Load initial value into TREG4L (low byte) and TREG4H (high byte)
- Enable with `SET 7, (T16RUN)` and `SET 0, (T16RUN)`
- Read current value from TREG4L:TREG4H (16-bit counter)
- Timer counts up/down based on mode

**Note:** The 16-bit registers require special encoding in ASL assembler:
```asm
db 0Ah, 90h, 01h, 00h  ; LDW (TREG4L:24), 0x0001  (ASL unsupported)
```

1. **Register definitions:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/shared/sfr_tmp94c241.asm` (lines 65-125)
2. **Boot initialization:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/shared/boot_hw_init.asm` (lines 66-82)
3. **Sub CPU boot:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/subcpu/boot/kn5000_subcpu_boot.asm` (lines 99-131, 263-317)
4. **Sub CPU program:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-roms-disasm/subcpu/kn5000_subprogram_v142.asm` (lines 9330-9334)
5. **Documentation:** `/home/fsanches/devel/kn5000-docs/reverse-engineering.md` (lines 840-932)

### Recommended Timer for Elapsed Time Measurement

**Use 16-bit Timer 4 (T4)** because:
1. Already initialized in boot sequence with known configuration
2. 16-bit resolution (up to 65535 counts)
3. Register addresses are well-documented
4. Can be read at any time without stopping the timer
5. Doesn't interfere with other timers (T0-T3 handle different functions)

# Virtual Machine Timing Analysis

## pauseThread Implementation

The `op_pauseThread()` function is straightforward:

```cpp
void VirtualMachine::op_pauseThread() {
	debug(DBG_VM, "VirtualMachine::op_pauseThread()");
	gotoNextThread = true;
}
```

This simply sets a flag to advance to the next thread, effectively pausing the current execution thread.

## Delay Value and Frame Timing

The frame timing mechanism uses `VM_VARIABLE_PAUSE_SLICES`:

```cpp
int32_t delay = sys->getTimeStamp() - lastTimeStamp;
int32_t timeToSleep = vmVariables[VM_VARIABLE_PAUSE_SLICES] * 20 - delay;
```

**Key timing details:**
- Each pause slice represents **20 milliseconds**
- The bytecode sets `VM_VARIABLE_PAUSE_SLICES` from 1 to 5
- This value determines how long an image displays before advancing
- The system calculates elapsed time and sleeps accordingly to maintain consistent frame pacing

This creates variable frame delays ranging from 20ms to 100ms depending on the scriptable pause slice value.

1→# Another World VM Port - Key Notes
     2→
     3→## Architecture
     4→- **ASL assembler** (`cpu 96c141`): TLCS-900/H target
     5→- **Bytecode is big-endian** (Amiga/68k origin), TLCS-900 is little-endian → use `EX W, A` to byte-swap after `LD WA, (XIX)` for fetch_word
     6→- **LDIRW** uses XHL=src, XDE=dst, XBC=word_count (not XIX/XIY!)
     7→- `AND (XIY), WA` assembles as 16-bit AND (ASL determines size from register)
     8→- `ADDW`/`SUBW` for explicit word-size memory operations
     9→
    10→## VM Execution Model
    11→- `_end_of_EXECUTE_INSTRUCTION`: computes VM_PC from XIX offset → XIX must point to bytecode
    12→- `_after_PC_update`: skips VM_PC recomputation → use when VM_PC was already set (JMP, CALL, RET, NEXT_THREAD)
    13→- **Critical**: opcodes that replace XIX with non-bytecode pointers (0x80, 0x40 video) must save VM_PC BEFORE the replacement and use `_after_PC_update`
    14→- Same issue for pauseThread: after NEXT_THREAD sets VM_PC, must use `_after_PC_update`
    15→
    16→## Helper Functions
    17→- `_read_vm_var`: Input A=index, Output DE=value, Clobbers XIY/XWA

## Frame Timing in Another World VM - Research Report

Based on my investigation of the reference implementation and the current KN5000 port, here's a complete analysis of how frame timing works:

### Key Finding: VM_VARIABLE_PAUSE_SLICES (Variable 0xFF)

From Fabien Sanglard's reference implementation, the Another World VM uses a **variable-duration frame timing mechanism** based on variable `0xFF`:

**Timing Unit:** Each frame's duration is measured in **20-millisecond slices**
- The bytecode writes a value (1-5) to variable `0xFF`
- Each unit represents **20ms** of display time
- This gives frame durations from:
  - **1 slice = 20ms (50 Hz)**
  - **2 slices = 40ms (25 Hz)**
  - **3 slices = 60ms (16.67 Hz)**
  - **4 slices = 80ms (12.5 Hz)**
  - **5 slices = 100ms (10 Hz)**

**Timing Calculation:**
```
timeToSleep = vmVariables[0xFF] * 20 - elapsedTime
```

The reference implementation uses:
```cpp
int32_t delay = sys->getTimeStamp() - lastTimeStamp;
int32_t timeToSleep = vmVariables[VM_VARIABLE_PAUSE_SLICES] * 20 - delay;
```

### How pauseThread Works

The `pauseThread` (opcode 0x06) instruction:
1. Does NOT directly use a delay value
2. Simply sets `gotoNextThread = true` to pause the current thread
3. Advances to the next active thread in the thread scheduler
4. The actual frame delay happens at the **frame boundary** via the PAUSE function

The VM variables related to timing:
- **Variable 0xFF (VM_VARIABLE_PAUSE_SLICES):** Controls how many 20ms slices the current frame should display
- **Variable 0x50:** Used for hero position tracking (not timing-related)

### Current Implementation Status in KN5000

**What's already implemented:**
- `PAUSE` function at line 392-399: Performs a CPU delay loop
- `LONG_PAUSE` function at line 383-390: Performs a longer delay
- Frame boundary detection: Calls `PAUSE` after `UPDATE_DISPLAY` (opcode 0x10)

**What's MISSING:**
- VM_VARIABLE_PAUSE_SLICES (0xFF) is **not defined** as a constant in the code
- The `PAUSE` function uses **fixed delays** (BC=0, DE=1) but does **not read variable 0xFF**
- No implementation of the 20ms-per-slice timing calculation
- The delay loops appear to be calibration-based rather than slice-based

**Current PAUSE implementation (line 392-399):**
```asm
PAUSE:
    LD BC, 0
PAUSE_LOOP1:
    LD DE, 01h
PAUSE_LOOP2:
    DJNZ DE, PAUSE_LOOP2
    DJNZ BC, PAUSE_LOOP1
    RET
```

This is a fixed delay loop, not reading variable 0xFF.

### What Needs to Be Done

To implement proper frame timing per the Another World VM specification:

1. **Add the constant definition:**
   ```asm
   VM_VARIABLE_PAUSE_SLICES EQU 0FFh
   ```

2. **Modify PAUSE to read variable 0xFF:**
   - Read VM variable 0xFF using `_read_vm_var`
   - Calculate delay in microseconds/CPU cycles
   - Use the slice value to determine loop count
   - Default to 1 slice (20ms) if variable is 0 or unset

3. **Calibrate the delay loop:**
   - The CPU runs at 25 MHz
   - 20ms delay = 500,000 cycles
   - Need to account for instruction timing to calibrate the nested loop

### References

From Fabien Sanglard's implementation documentation:
> "A virtual machine frame has a variable duration. The unit of time is 20ms and the frame can be set to live for 1 (20ms ; 50Hz) up to 5 (100ms ; 10Hz)."
> "The vm actually write for how long a video frame should be displayed in variable 0xFF. The value is the number of 20ms slice."

Sources:
- [Fabien Sanglard's Another World Bytecode Interpreter](https://github.com/fabiensanglard/Another-World-Bytecode-Interpreter)
- [Another World Source Code Review](https://fabiensanglard.net/anotherWorld_code_review/)

	LD A, 067h
	CALL _read_vm_var	; DE = vm_var[0x67]
	CP DE, 1
	JP NE, _blit_no_hack

	CP A, 11h
	JP NE, INSTRUCTION_IS_NOT_KILL_THREAD
	LD WA, 0
	LD A, (CURRENT_THREAD)
	SLA 2, WA

	include "tmp94c241.inc"

; EXTENSION: Uses 512KB extension board SRAM at 0x200000-0x27FFFF
	ifdef TARGET_MAINCPU
	ORG 010000h
	endif
	ifdef TARGET_EXTENSION
	ORG 0200000h
	endif

POLYGON_XMIN:	DW ?						; int16_t
POLYGON_XMAX:	DW ?						; int16_t
POLYGON_YMIN:	DW ?						; int16_t
POLYGON_YMAX:	DW ?						; int16_t
HLINEY:		DW ?							; int16_t
CUR_LINE:			; uint32_t

CPT1:				; uint32_t

; Include shared VGA I/O and initialization routines
	include "vga_io.asm"
	include "vga_init.asm"
	ret			; VGA_Setup has no ret (designed for inline use)

; Entry Point - Called after hardware reset
Reset_Handler:
	include "boot_hw_init.asm"

	; Set up stack pointer (after hardware init)
	LDA_XWA_IMM24 STACK_TOP
	ld XSP, XWA

	; Initialize VGA display using shared code
	CALR VGA_Setup

	; Turn screen on (sequencer clocking mode)
	VGA_SEQUENCER 01h, 001h

	jp ENTRY

	endif ; TARGET_MAINCPU

; =============================================================================
; Extension Board ROM Layout
; =============================================================================
	ifdef TARGET_EXTENSION

	ORG 0280000h

EXTENSION_HEADER:
	db 'XAPR'
	dd POINTERS
	JP ENTRY
POINTERS:
	db 0Eh, 00h, 00h, 00h; EMPTY_ROUTINE
	db 0Eh, 00h, 00h, 00h; EMPTY_ROUTINE
	db 0Eh, 00h, 00h, 00h; EMPTY_ROUTINE
	db 0Eh, 00h, 00h, 00h; EMPTY_ROUTINE
	db 0Eh, 00h, 00h, 00h; EMPTY_ROUTINE

	endif ; TARGET_EXTENSION

; =============================================================================
; VM Code (shared between both targets)
; =============================================================================
	include "another_world_vm.asm"

; =============================================================================
; ROM End (target-specific)
; =============================================================================
	ifdef TARGET_MAINCPU

Default_Handler:
	halt
	jr Default_Handler

; Reset Handler Location
	ORG 0FFFEE0h
Reset_Entry:
	jp Reset_Handler

; Fill gap between reset entry and vector table
	ORG 0FFFEE4h
	rept 01Ch
	db 0FFh
	endm

; Interrupt Vector Table
	ORG 0FFFF00h
VECTOR_TABLE:
	dd 00FFFEE0h		; Vector 0: Reset
	dd Default_Handler	; Vector 1
	dd Default_Handler	; Vector 2
	dd Default_Handler	; Vector 3
	dd Default_Handler	; Vector 4
	dd Default_Handler	; Vector 5
	dd Default_Handler	; Vector 6
	dd Default_Handler	; Vector 7

	; === Watchdog Timer Disable ===

	LD (WDCR), 0b1h

	; === System Clock Setup ===
	LD (CLKMOD), 004h			; High-speed (25 MHz)

	; === Data Bus Ports Setup (P2, P3, P7) ===
	; REVIEW: May be needed for external bus access to VGA/VRAM

	LD (P3FC), 0ffh
	LD (P7), 0ffh
	LD (P7FC), 01fh

	; === Address Bus Ports Setup (PA, PB, PC, PD, PE, PH, PZ) ===
	; REVIEW: May be needed for address lines to reach 0x170000 (VGA)
	; and 0x1A0000 (VRAM). Safe to keep; test removal in MAME.
	LD (PA), 0feh
	LD (PAFC), 008h
	LD (PB), 0ffh
	LD (PBFC), 01fh
	LD (PC), 003h
	LD (PCFC), 000h
	LD (PCCR), 002h

### SYSTEM_TIMESTAMP Source

`SYSTEM_TIMESTAMP` (address 0x0409) is a 32-bit counter incremented by the Timer 1 interrupt handler (`INTT1_HANDLER` at 0xEF0BF9). The timer is configured during system initialization:

```asm
; Timer configuration at EF042D
LD (T01MOD), 01dh   ; Timer 0/1 mode: cascade mode, T32 source
LD (TREG0), 00ah    ; Timer 0 reload = 10
LD (TREG1), 010h    ; Timer 1 reload = 16
SET 1, (T8RUN)      ; Start Timer 1
```

Each `SYSTEM_TIMESTAMP` tick represents approximately **1 millisecond** based on the Timer 0/1 cascade configuration with the 20 MHz system clock.

### Delay Formula

```
Actual_delay_ms = WA / 2
```

### Common FDC Delay Values

| WA Value | Effective Delay | Usage Context |
|----------|-----------------|---------------|
| 2        | ~1 ms           | Brief settling (FDC_INIT, FDC_STATUS_HANDLER) |

    71→	CP WA, (X2)
    72→	JP GT, XMAX_OK
    73→	LD WA, (X2)
    74→XMAX_OK:
    75→	LD (LINE_XMAX), WA

    77→	; int16_t xmin = MIN(x1, x2);
    78→	LD WA, (X1)
    79→	CP WA, (X2)

    95→	; 	m_curPagePtr1->pix(m_hliney, x) = color;
    96→	LD XIX, (CUR_LINE)
    97→	LD HL, (LINE_XMIN)
    98→	EXTS XHL
    99→	ADD XIX, XHL

   107→	DJNZ HL, drawLineN_loop
   108→	
   109→	POP XHL

   111→	RET

   115→	PUSH XIX
   116→	PUSH XIY
   117→	PUSH XHL
   118→

1→# TMP94C241C Peripherals Reference
     2→
     3→## Table of Contents
     4→1. [8-Bit Timers](#8-bit-timers)
     5→2. [16-Bit Timers](#16-bit-timers)
     6→3. [Serial Channels](#serial-channels)
     7→4. [ADC](#adc)
     8→5. [DAC](#dac)
     9→6. [Watchdog Timer](#watchdog-timer)
    10→7. [Memory Controller](#memory-controller)
    11→8. [DRAM Controller](#dram-controller)
    12→
    13→---
    14→
    15→## 8-Bit Timers
    16→
    17→Four 8-bit timers (T0-T3) with modes:
    18→- 8-bit interval timer (4 channels)
    19→- 16-bit interval timer (2 channels, cascaded)
    20→- 8-bit PPG output (2 channels)
    21→- 8-bit PWM output (2 channels)
    22→
    23→### Prescaler
    24→
    25→9-bit prescaler generates timer clocks from fc/4:
    26→- φT1 = fc/4 (0.2μs @ 20MHz)
    27→- φT4 = fc/16 (0.8μs @ 20MHz)
    28→- φT16 = fc/64 (3.2μs @ 20MHz)
    29→- φT256 = fc/1024 (51.2μs @ 20MHz)
    30→
    31→Control: T16RUN<PRRUN> (1=run, 0=stop/clear)
    32→
    33→### 8-Bit Interval Timer Mode
    34→
    35→Each timer counts up using selected clock. Match with TREGn generates interrupt and optionally inverts flip-flop.
    36→
    37→**Setup:**
    38→1. Stop timer (T8RUN<TnRUN>=0)
    39→2. Set mode in T01MOD/T23MOD
    40→3. Set interval in TREGn
    41→4. Configure flip-flop in TFFCR if needed
    42→5. Start timer (T8RUN<TnRUN>=1)
    43→
    44→**Interval calculation:**
    45→```
    46→Interval = TREGn × clock_period
    47→```
    48→
    49→### 16-Bit Timer Mode (Cascaded)
    50→
    51→Timer 0+1 or Timer 2+3 cascaded:
    52→- Lower timer (0 or 2) overflow clocks upper timer
    53→- 16-bit interval = TREG1:TREG0 or TREG3:TREG2
    54→
    55→**Write order:** Set TREG0 first (disables compare), then TREG1 (enables compare).
    56→
    57→### PPG Mode (Programmable Pulse Generation)
    58→
    59→Variable frequency/duty square wave output.
    60→- Timer 0 → TO1 (PC0)
    61→- Timer 2 → TO3 (PC1)
    62→
    63→```
    64→High time = TREGn × clock
    65→Low time = (TREGn+1 - TREGn) × clock
    66→Period = (TREGn+1) × clock
    67→```
    68→
    69→### PWM Mode
    70→
    71→8-bit resolution PWM:
    72→- Timer 0 → TO1, Timer 2 → TO3
    73→- Counter cycles 0 to 2^n-1 (n=7 or 8)
    74→- Output high while count < TREGn
    75→
    76→---
    77→
    78→## 16-Bit Timers
    79→
    80→Four 16-bit timer/event counters (T4, T6, T8, TA) with modes:
    81→- Interval timer
    82→- Event counter
    83→- PPG output
    84→- Capture (frequency/pulse measurement)
    85→- Phase output
    86→
    87→### Timer Structure
    88→
    89→Each timer has:
    90→- 16-bit up counter (UC4/6/8/A)
    91→- Two 16-bit timer registers (TREG4/5, etc.)
    92→- Two 16-bit capture registers (CAP4/5, etc.)
    93→- Timer flip-flop (TFF4/6/8/A)
    94→- Optional second flip-flop (TFF7/B for T6/TA)
    95→
    96→### Clock Sources
    97→
    98→| T4CLK | Source |
    99→|-------|--------|
   100→| 00 | TI4 external |
   101→| 01 | φT1 |
   102→| 10 | φT4 |
   103→| 11 | φT16 |
   104→
   105→### 16-Bit Interval Timer Mode
   106→
   107→**Setup:**
   108→1. Stop timer
   109→2. Set clock source in TnMOD
   110→3. Set interval in TREG5/7/9/B (clears counter on match)
   111→4. Enable interrupt/flip-flop as needed
   112→5. Start timer
   113→
   114→### Event Counter Mode
   115→
   116→Count external pulses on TIn pin:
   117→- Set TnCLK = 00 for external clock
   118→- Each rising edge increments counter
   119→
   120→### Capture Mode
   121→
   122→Capture counter value on external trigger:
   123→- Software capture: Write to TnMOD<CAPnIN>
   124→- External capture: Edge on TIn pin
   125→
   126→**Applications:**
   127→- Frequency measurement
   128→- Pulse width measurement
   129→- Time interval measurement
   130→
   131→### PPG Mode
   132→
   133→Variable duty/frequency output:
   134→- TREGn sets high→low transition
   135→- TREGn+1 sets low→high and counter clear
   136→- Condition: TREGn < TREGn+1
   137→
   138→### Phase Output Mode
   139→
   140→Timer 6 and Timer A have two flip-flops for phase output:
   141→- TFF6/TFF7 independently controlled
   142→- Output signals with programmable phase difference
   143→
   144→---
   145→
   146→## Serial Channels
   147→
   148→Two full-duplex serial channels with modes:
   149→- Mode 0: I/O interface (synchronous)
   150→- Mode 1: 7-bit UART
   151→- Mode 2: 8-bit UART
   152→- Mode 3: 9-bit UART
   153→
   154→### Baud Rate
   155→
   156→Baud rate generator divides prescaler output:
   157→
   158→```
   159→Baud = φTx / (BRnK × 16)
   160→
   161→φTx selection:
   162→  00 = φT0 (fc/4)
   163→  01 = φT2 (fc/16)
   164→  10 = φT8 (fc/64)
   165→  11 = φT32 (fc/256)
   166→```
   167→
   168→**Common baud rates at 20MHz:**
   169→
   170→| Baud | φTx | BRnK |
   171→|------|-----|------|
   172→| 9600 | φT8 | 13 |
   173→| 19200 | φT8 | 6-7 |
   174→| 38400 | φT2 | 13 |
   175→| 115200 | φT0 | 11 |
   176→
   177→### I/O Interface Mode (Mode 0)
   178→
   179→Synchronous serial for shift register expansion:
   180→- SCLK output mode: Internal clock drives SCLK pin
   181→- SCLK input mode: External clock on SCLK pin
   182→- 8 bits per frame, LSB first
   183→
   184→### UART Modes (Mode 1-3)
   185→
   186→Asynchronous serial with start/stop bits:
   187→- Mode 1: 7 data + optional parity
   188→- Mode 2: 8 data + optional parity
   189→- Mode 3: 9 data (for multi-processor)
   190→
   191→**Frame format:**
   192→```
   193→[Start][D0][D1]...[Dn][Parity?][Stop]
   194→```
   195→
   196→### Error Detection
   197→
   198→- OERR: Overrun error (new data before read)
   199→- PERR: Parity error
   200→- FERR: Framing error (no stop bit)
   201→
   202→Read SCnCR to check, errors cleared on read.
   203→
   204→### Handshaking
   205→
   206→CTS input for flow control:
   207→- Set SCnMOD<CTSE>=1
   208→- Transmission pauses when CTS high
   209→
   210→---
   211→
   212→## ADC
   213→
   214→10-bit successive approximation ADC with 8 channels.
   215→
   216→### Features
   217→
   218→- 8 analog inputs (AN0-AN7 / Port G)
   219→- Sample-and-hold circuit
   220→- Single or scan conversion
   221→- Repeat mode
   222→
   223→### Conversion Speed
   224→
   225→| SPEED | States | Time @ 20MHz |
   226→|-------|--------|--------------|
   227→| 00 | 160 | 8 μs |
   228→| 01 | 104 | 5.2 μs |
   229→| 10 | 88 | 4.4 μs |
   230→| 11 | 72 | 3.6 μs |
   231→
   232→### Operating Modes
   233→
   234→**Single mode:** Convert one channel, stop.
   235→
   236→**Scan mode:** Convert channels AN0-ANn sequentially.
   237→
   238→**Repeat mode:** Continuous conversion.
   239→
   240→### Setup
   241→
   242→1. Enable ADC (ADMOD2<ADCE>=1)
   243→2. Enable reference (ADMOD2<VREFON>=1)
   244→3. Wait stabilization time
   245→4. Select channel/mode in ADMOD1
   246→5. Start conversion (ADMOD1<ADS>=1)
   247→6. Wait for EOCF or INTAD interrupt
   248→7. Read result from ADREGxxH/L
   249→
   250→### Result Registers
   251→
   252→Results are 10-bit, stored in pairs:
   253→- ADREG04: AN0 or AN4
   254→- ADREG15: AN1 or AN5
   255→- ADREG26: AN2 or AN6
   256→- ADREG37: AN3 or AN7
   257→
   258→```
   259→ADREGxxH[7:6] = result[9:8]
   260→ADREGxxL[7:0] = result[7:0]
   261→```
   262→
   263→---
   264→
   265→## DAC
   266→
   267→Two 8-bit voltage output DACs with buffer amplifiers.
   268→
   269→### Output Voltage
   270→
   271→```
   272→Vout = (DAREG / 256) × VREFH
   273→```
   274→
   275→### Setup
   276→
   277→1. Write value to DAREG0 or DAREG1
   278→2. Enable output: DADRV<DA0DR>=1 or <DA1DR>=1
   279→
   280→Output goes to Hi-Z when disabled.
   281→
   282→---
   283→
   284→## Watchdog Timer
   285→
   286→Runaway detection timer for system recovery.
   287→
   288→### Operation
   289→
   290→22-bit binary counter clocked by φ (2/fc).
   291→Overflow triggers INTWD interrupt and WDTOUT pin low.
   292→
   293→### Detection Times
   294→
   295→| WDTP | Cycles | Time @ 20MHz |
   296→|------|--------|--------------|
   297→| 00 | 2^16 | 6.6 ms |
   298→| 01 | 2^18 | 26.2 ms |
   299→| 10 | 2^20 | 104.9 ms |
   300→| 11 | 2^22 | 419.4 ms |
   301→
   302→### Usage
   303→
   304→1. Enable: WDMOD<WDTE>=1
   305→2. Periodically clear: Write 4EH to WDCR
   306→3. If software fails to clear, WDT overflows
   307→
   308→### HALT Mode
   309→
   310→WDMOD<HALTM> selects HALT behavior:
   311→- 00: RUN (CPU stops, WDT continues)
   312→- 01: STOP (all clocks stop)
   313→- 10: IDLE (oscillator runs, peripherals stop)
   314→
   315→---
   316→
   317→## Memory Controller
   318→
   319→6-block address area controller for external memory.
   320→
   321→### Block Configuration
   322→
   323→Each block has:
   324→- Start address (MSARn)
   325→- Size mask (MAMRn)
   326→- Control settings (BnCSL/H)
   327→
   328→### Memory Types
   329→
   330→| BnOM | Type |
   331→|------|------|
   332→| 00 | SRAM/ROM |
   333→| 01 | DRAM (blocks 1,3 only) |
   334→
   335→### Data Bus Width
   336→
   337→| BnBUS | Width |
   338→|-------|-------|
   339→| 00 | 8-bit |
   340→| 01 | 16-bit |
   341→| 10 | 32-bit |
   342→
   343→### Wait States
   344→
   345→BnWR/BnWW set read/write waits:
   346→- 000: 2 states (100ns @ 20MHz)
   347→- 001: 3 states
   348→- ...
   349→- 101: 7 states
   350→- 110: WAIT pin input
   351→- 111: WAIT pin input
   352→
   353→### Chip Select
   354→
   355→6 chip select outputs (CS0-CS5) directly from Port 8.
   356→Active when corresponding block is accessed.
   357→
   358→---
   359→
   360→## DRAM Controller
   361→
   362→Two-channel DRAM controller for blocks 1 and 3.
   363→
   364→### Supported Configurations
   365→
   366→- 1CAS (8-bit bus)
   367→- 2CAS (16-bit bus)
   368→- 4CAS (32-bit bus, channel 1 only)
   369→- Page mode access
   370→
   371→### Address Multiplexing
   372→
   373→MUX bits set row/column address split based on DRAM size.
   374→
   375→### Refresh Modes
   376→
   377→**CAS-before-RAS interval refresh:**
   378→- Automatic refresh at programmable intervals
   379→- RS bits select interval (78-384 cycles)
   380→
   381→**Self-refresh:**
   382→- For STOP mode power saving
   383→- Set SFRC=0 before HALT
   384→
   385→**Dummy refresh:**
   386→- Manual refresh for initialization
   387→
   388→### Timing
   389→
   390→Minimum 3 states for DRAM access. Page mode can be 2 states for sequential access within same row.
   391→
   392→### Bus Release
   393→
   394→BRM bit controls behavior during bus release:
   395→- BRM=0: Release DRAM pins too
   396→- BRM=1: Maintain DRAM pins for refresh
   397→

1→# TMP94C241C Interrupt System Reference
     2→
     3→## Overview
     4→
     5→38 interrupt sources total:
     6→- 2 CPU interrupts (SWI, illegal instruction)
     7→- 10 external (NMI, INT0, INT4-INTB)
     8→- 18 internal peripheral
     9→- 8 micro DMA channels
    10→
    11→---
    12→
    13→## Interrupt Vector Table
    14→
    15→Vectors at FFFF00H + vector_number.
    16→
    17→| Vector | Address | Source | Description |
    18→|--------|---------|--------|-------------|
    19→| 00H | FFFF00H | Reset | Reset vector |
    20→| 04H | FFFF04H | — | Default (invalid) |
    21→| 08H | FFFF08H | SWI 0 | Software interrupt 0 |
    22→| 09H | FFFF09H | SWI 1 | Software interrupt 1 |
    23→| 0AH | FFFF0AH | SWI 2 | Software interrupt 2 |
    24→| 0BH | FFFF0BH | SWI 3 | Software interrupt 3 |

## Frame Lifecycle Analysis - Another World VM on KN5000

Based on my analysis of `/home/fsanches/devel/custom-kn5000-roms/anotherworld/src/another_world_vm.asm` and `/home/fsanches/devel/custom-kn5000-roms/anotherworld/src/main.asm`, here's the complete frame lifecycle:

### Frame Boundaries

**A "frame" spans from:**
- **Start**: Return from `CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS` (after part switch check and thread state updates)
- **End**: When thread scanning wraps around from thread 63 to thread 0 in `NEXT_THREAD`

**Exact frame boundary code (lines 1185-1200):**
```asm
NEXT_THREAD:
    CALL INPUT_UPDATE_PLAYER          ; Frame starts here

    LD WA, 0
    LD A, (CURRENT_THREAD)

_next_thread__do_loop:
    INC A
    CP A, 64
    JP NE, _not_end_of_frame
    ; == END OF FRAME ==
    LDB (CURRENT_THREAD), 0
    CALL CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS        ; Part switches, thread state commits
    LD A, 0FEh
    CALL UPDATE_DISPLAY               ; Blit framebuffer to VGA
    LD A, 0
_not_end_of_frame:
    ; ... continue thread scanning ...
```

### Where PAUSE is Called

**PAUSE is called from exactly 2 locations:**

1. **Line 226 (BREAK function)** - appears to be a temporary diagnostic function:
```asm
BREAK:
    LD A, 0FEh
    CALL UPDATE_DISPLAY
    CALL PAUSE          ; Frame timing delay
    RET
```

2. **Line 1989 (BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER opcode 0x10)** - the main frame timing point:
```asm
INSTRUCTION_BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER:       ; Opcode 0x10
    LD A, (XIX)         ; byte pageId
    INC XIX
    ; ... part switch hack ...
    CALL UPDATE_DISPLAY             ; Blit specified page
    CALL PAUSE                       ; Frame timing delay
    JP _end_of_EXECUTE_INSTRUCTION
```

### Frame Timing Paths

There are **two distinct frame timing patterns**:

**Path A: Via BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER (Opcode 0x10)** [Most common]
- Bytecode calls opcode 0x10 with a page ID
- `UPDATE_DISPLAY` blits that page to VGA
- `PAUSE` implements frame delay
- Returns to main execution loop

**Path B: Via NEXT_THREAD end-of-frame path** [Frame boundary]
- When thread scanning wraps (A reaches 64), frame boundary is detected
- `CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS` is called (part switches, thread state commits)
- `UPDATE_DISPLAY` blits page 0xFE (end-of-frame marker)
- **No PAUSE here** — execution immediately continues to find next active thread
- Next opcode executes without additional delay

### Key Discovery: NEXT_THREAD Does NOT Pause

The `NEXT_THREAD` end-of-frame path (lines 1195-1200) calls `UPDATE_DISPLAY` but **NOT `PAUSE`**. This means:
- The bytecode is responsible for frame pacing via explicit BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER calls
- The VM's internal thread-switching frame boundary is a bookkeeping event, not a frame timing event
- Frame timing is entirely controlled by bytecode (game logic)

### Variable 0xFF (Pause Slices)

**Status: NOT CURRENTLY USED**

Search results show variable 0xFF is not referenced anywhere in the codebase. The only related grep match was color value 0xFF (black), not the pause slices variable. This means:
- Pause timing is currently **hardcoded** via the simple `PAUSE` loop (lines 392-399)
- No VM variable controls frame timing
- No "pause slices" concept is implemented

### Current PAUSE Implementation

**Lines 392-399:**
```asm
PAUSE:
    LD BC, 0
PAUSE_LOOP1:
    LD DE, 01h          ; Inner loop count = 1
PAUSE_LOOP2:
    DJNZ DE, PAUSE_LOOP2
    DJNZ BC, PAUSE_LOOP1
    RET
```

This is a **fixed 65,536-instruction busy-loop** (BC starts at 0x10000 after `LD BC, 0`), providing constant frame delay. The delay is NOT controlled by:
- VM variables
- Game state
- Elapsed time
- Timer hardware

### Where Frame Start Time Should Be Recorded

**Recommended location: Line 1186, right after NEXT_THREAD entry:**

```asm

    CALL INPUT_UPDATE_PLAYER

    ; <-- RECORD FRAME START TIME HERE (before any thread work)

    ; - Record cycle counter

    LD WA, 0
    LD A, (CURRENT_THREAD)
```

This captures the true frame boundary **before** any thread execution, thread state updates, or display operations.

### Memory Layout for Timer Variables

# Plan: Fix Polygon Rendering Glitches

## Context

The Another World VM port on KN5000 shows a grey screen with correct palette but **no visible polygon content**. After analyzing the polygon rendering pipeline against the reference MAME HLE implementation, three bugs were found that cause incorrect rendering and potential memory corruption.

**File to modify:** `src/another_world_vm.asm`

## Bug #1: drawLine off-by-one (causes buffer overflow/corruption)

**Location:** `drawLineN` (line 101), `drawLineP` (line 140), `drawLineBlend` (line 167)

**Problem:** Loop count `HL = xmax - xmin` is used with `DJNZ HL`, which decrements-then-tests. This draws `xmax - xmin` pixels instead of `xmax - xmin + 1` (inclusive range).

**Critical case:** When `xmax == xmin` (single pixel), `HL = 0`. DJNZ decrements to `0xFFFF` (non-zero), causing 65,536 iterations — massive buffer overflow that corrupts all VM state. This is likely the root cause of the rendering failure.

**Fix:** Add `INC HL` after `SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)` in all three functions:

- `drawLineN` line 101: `SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)` → add `INC HL` after
- `drawLineP` line 140: `SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)` → add `INC HL` after
- `drawLineBlend` line 167: `SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)` → add `INC HL` after

## Bug #2: fillPolygon hliney > 199 jumps to wrong label

**Location:** `fillPolygon` line 716-717

**Problem:** When `HLINEY > 199`, the code jumps to `POLYGON_RASTER_LOOP` which continues processing the next polygon segment. The reference code does `return` (exits the entire fillPolygon function). This causes polygons that extend below the screen to continue rendering with wrong edge parameters, producing garbage.

**Current code:**
```asm
CPW (HLINEY), 199
JP GT, POLYGON_RASTER_LOOP    ; BUG: continues with next segment
```

**Fix:**
```asm
CPW (HLINEY), 199
JP GT, end_of_fillPolygon      ; EXIT: stop rendering this polygon
```

## Bug #3: drawPoint writes to wrong location and size

**Location:** `drawPoint` lines 181-192

**Problem (3 issues):**
1. Writes to hardcoded VRAM address `0x1A0000` instead of `CUR_PAGE_PTR_1` (page buffer)
2. `LD (XIX), BC` writes 2 bytes instead of 1 (writes color C + garbage B)
3. `LD WA, 0` doesn't clear upper XWA bits; subsequent `MUL XWA, 320` may use garbage upper bits (actually MUL XWA,DE does WA×DE→XWA so upper bits get overwritten — but XDE upper bits from `ADD XWA, XDE` are still garbage)

**Fix:** Replace with:
```asm
drawPoint:
    PUSH XIX
    LD XWA, 0
    LD WA, HL              ; XWA = y (zero-extended 32-bit)
    LD DE, 320
    MUL XWA, DE            ; XWA = y * 320
    EXTZ XDE               ; zero-extend x to 32-bit
    ADD XWA, XDE           ; XWA = y*320 + x
    LD XIX, (CUR_PAGE_PTR_1)
    ADD XIX, XWA
    LDB (XIX), C           ; write 1 byte (color)
    POP XIX
    RET
```

## Verification

1. `make clean && make` — must build without errors
2. `make test` — run in MAME, verify polygon content appears on screen after setPalette
3. The intro cinematic should show the Interplay logo and opening sequence polygons instead of a solid grey screen

# Plan: Timer-Based Frame Timing with Overrun Detection

## Context

The Another World intro plays slowly in some scenes. The current frame timing uses a fixed busy-wait loop (`PAUSE`) that ignores the VM's `variable[0xFF]` (pause slices), which specifies how many 20ms slices each frame should display. Additionally, there's no way to identify which frames exceed their time budget, making performance optimization blind.

**Goal:** Use TMP94C241F hardware timers for precise frame pacing, and add visible diagnostics for frame overruns.

## How AW Frame Timing Should Work (Reference)

The VM bytecode writes a value (typically 1-5) to variable `0xFF` specifying frame duration in 20ms slices:
- 1 slice = 20ms (50 Hz), 2 slices = 40ms (25 Hz), etc.

The reference implementation: `timeToSleep = var[0xFF] * 20ms - elapsedTime`. If elapsed > target, the frame overran (no sleep).

Currently, `PAUSE` is a fixed ~65K-iteration busy-loop called from `BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER` (opcode 0x10). It doesn't read var 0xFF and has no concept of elapsed time.

## Files to Modify

- `src/boot_hw_init.asm` — Add T0/T1 timer cascade initialization
- `src/main.asm` — Add INTT1 ISR, extend vector table, add RAM variables
- `src/another_world_vm.asm` — Rewrite PAUSE, record frame start time, add overrun indicator

## Step 1: Timer Hardware Setup (`src/boot_hw_init.asm`)

Add T0/T1 cascade timer initialization (same config as original KN5000 firmware). At the end of boot_hw_init.asm, before the implicit return:

```asm
; === 8-bit Timer Setup (T0/T1 cascade for system tick) ===
LD (T01MOD), 01dh       ; T0: T32 clock (fSYS/32), T1: cascade from T0
LD (T02FFCR), 000h      ; No flip-flop
LD (TREG0), 00ah        ; T0 divides by 10
LD (TREG1), 010h        ; T1 divides by 16
LD (TRDC), 000h         ; No double-buffer
SET 1, (T8RUN)          ; Start T0+T1

; Enable INTT1 interrupt at priority level 6
LD (INTET01), 0C0h      ; bits [7:5] = 110 = level 6, INTT0 disabled
```

**Tick rate at 25 MHz:** fSYS/32 = 781,250 Hz → ÷10 (T0) → ÷16 (T1) = **4,882.8 Hz** (~204.8 µs per tick).

**20ms = ~98 ticks.** Pre-computed constant: `TICKS_PER_SLICE EQU 98`

## Step 2: Interrupt Handler and Vector Table (`src/main.asm`)

**ISR** (minimal, placed before or after `Default_Handler`):

```asm
INTT1_Handler:
    PUSH XWA
    LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
    INC 1, XWA              ; 32-bit increment
    LD (SYSTEM_TICKS), XWA
    POP XWA
    RETI
```

**Extend vector table** from 8 entries to 22 (covers through offset 0x54 = INTT1):

```asm
ORG 0FFFF00h
VECTOR_TABLE:
    dd 00FFFEE0h           ; 0x00: Reset
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x04
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x08
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x0C
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x10
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x14
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x18
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x1C
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x20
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x24
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x28: INT0
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x2C: INT4
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x30: INT5
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x34: INT6
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x38: INT7
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x3C: reserved
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x40: INT8
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x44: INT9
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x48: INTA
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x4C: INTB
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x50: INTT0
    dd INTT1_Handler       ; 0x54: INTT1 ← our timer ISR
```

**Add RAM variables** (after `CUR_VIDEO_DATA` in the RAM section):

```asm
SYSTEM_TICKS:        DD ?   ; 32-bit tick counter (ISR-incremented, ~4883 Hz)
FRAME_START_TICKS:   DD ?   ; Tick count at frame start
LAST_FRAME_TICKS:    DW ?   ; Elapsed ticks of last frame (for diagnostics)
FRAME_OVERRAN:       DB ?   ; 1 if last frame exceeded budget, 0 otherwise
```

## Step 3: Enable Interrupts (`src/another_world_vm.asm`)

Change `EI 06` (disables all maskable interrupts) to `EI 0` (accepts all priority levels):

```asm
ENTRY:
    EI 0    ; Enable interrupts (was EI 06 = disabled)
```

This is safe because only INTT1 has a non-zero priority (level 6). All other interrupt sources default to priority 0 (disabled) after reset.

## Step 4: Record Frame Start Time (`src/another_world_vm.asm`)

In `NEXT_THREAD`, at the end-of-frame boundary (after `CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS`, before `UPDATE_DISPLAY`), record the frame start time for the **next** frame:

```asm
; == END OF FRAME ==
LDB (CURRENT_THREAD), 0
CALL CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS
LD A, 0FEh
CALL UPDATE_DISPLAY

; Record frame start time for next frame
LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
LD (FRAME_START_TICKS), XWA

LD A, 0
```

Also initialize `FRAME_START_TICKS` in `ENTRY` (before `MAIN_LOOP`):

```asm
LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
LD (FRAME_START_TICKS), XWA
```

## Step 5: Rewrite PAUSE (`src/another_world_vm.asm`)

Replace the fixed busy-loop with timer-based delay that reads VM variable 0xFF:

```asm
TICKS_PER_SLICE EQU 98     ; ~20ms at 4882.8 Hz tick rate

PAUSE:
    ; Read VM variable 0xFF (pause slices)
    PUSH XIX                ; save bytecode pointer
    LD A, 0FFh
    CALL _read_vm_var       ; DE = var[0xFF] (number of 20ms slices)

    ; Compute target ticks = slices * TICKS_PER_SLICE
    ; If slices == 0, use default of 1
    CP DE, 0
    JP NE, _pause_has_slices
    LD DE, 1
_pause_has_slices:
    LD WA, TICKS_PER_SLICE
    MUL XWA, DE             ; XWA = target_ticks (32-bit, but fits 16-bit)
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA  ; save target for reference (temporary, overwritten below)
    PUSH XWA                ; save target_ticks

    ; Compute elapsed = SYSTEM_TICKS - FRAME_START_TICKS
    LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
    LD XDE, (FRAME_START_TICKS)
    SUB XWA, XDE            ; XWA = elapsed ticks

    ; Check for overrun
    POP XDE                 ; XDE = target_ticks
    CP XWA, XDE
    JP UGE, _pause_overrun  ; elapsed >= target → overrun

    ; Wait for remaining time
    LD XBC, XDE             ; XBC = target_ticks
_pause_wait:
    LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
    LD XDE, (FRAME_START_TICKS)
    SUB XWA, XDE            ; XWA = elapsed
    CP XWA, XBC
    JP ULT, _pause_wait     ; keep waiting if elapsed < target

    ; Frame completed on time
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA   ; store actual elapsed
    LDB (FRAME_OVERRAN), 0
    POP XIX
    RET

_pause_overrun:
    ; Frame took longer than budget
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA   ; store actual elapsed
    LDB (FRAME_OVERRAN), 1
    POP XIX
    RET
```

## Step 6: Overrun Visual Indicator (`src/another_world_vm.asm`)

After `CALL PAUSE` in `BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER`, add a simple visual indicator — write a colored pixel at the top-right corner of the VGA framebuffer. Red (color index depends on current palette) for overrun, black for on-time:

```asm
; After CALL PAUSE in BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER:
LD A, (FRAME_OVERRAN)
CP A, 0
JP EQ, _no_overrun_indicator
; Overrun: write bright pixel at (319, 0)
LDB (001a0000h + 20*320 + 319), 0Fh   ; color 15 (white in most palettes)
JP _end_overrun_indicator
_no_overrun_indicator:
LDB (001a0000h + 20*320 + 319), 00h   ; color 0 (background)
_end_overrun_indicator:
```

This writes directly to VRAM at the top-right pixel after the blit, so it's visible on screen without affecting the page buffers.

## Verification

1. `make clean && make` — must build without errors
2. `make test` — run in MAME:
   - Verify the intro still plays correctly (timer didn't break anything)
   - Check if frame pacing feels more natural (scenes that were too slow should now use var 0xFF timing)
   - Look for white pixel flashes at top-right corner indicating frame overruns
3. In MAME debugger: examine `SYSTEM_TICKS` to verify timer is incrementing, `LAST_FRAME_TICKS` for frame durations, `FRAME_OVERRAN` for overrun detection

Add T0/T1 cascade timer initialization (same config as original KN5000 firmware). At the end of boot_hw_init.asm, before the implicit return:

```asm
; === 8-bit Timer Setup (T0/T1 cascade for system tick) ===
LD (T01MOD), 01dh       ; T0: T32 clock (fSYS/32), T1: cascade from T0
LD (T02FFCR), 000h      ; No flip-flop
LD (TREG0), 00ah        ; T0 divides by 10
LD (TREG1), 010h        ; T1 divides by 16
LD (TRDC), 000h         ; No double-buffer
SET 1, (T8RUN)          ; Start T0+T1

; Enable INTT1 interrupt at priority level 6
LD (INTET01), 0C0h      ; bits [7:5] = 110 = level 6, INTT0 disabled
```

**Tick rate at 25 MHz:** fSYS/32 = 781,250 Hz → ÷10 (T0) → ÷16 (T1) = **4,882.8 Hz** (~204.8 µs per tick).

**20ms = ~98 ticks.** Pre-computed constant: `TICKS_PER_SLICE EQU 98`

```asm
INTT1_Handler:
    PUSH XWA
    LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
    INC 1, XWA              ; 32-bit increment
    LD (SYSTEM_TICKS), XWA
    POP XWA
    RETI
```

VECTOR_TABLE:
    dd 00FFFEE0h           ; 0x00: Reset
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x04
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x08
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x0C
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x10
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x14
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x18
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x1C
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x20
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x24
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x28: INT0
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x2C: INT4
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x30: INT5
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x34: INT6
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x38: INT7
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x3C: reserved
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x40: INT8
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x44: INT9
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x48: INTA

    PUSH XWA                ; save target_ticks

    LD XDE, (FRAME_START_TICKS)

    CP XWA, XDE
    JP UGE, _pause_overrun  ; elapsed >= target → overrun

    ; Wait for remaining time
    LD XBC, XDE             ; XBC = target_ticks
_pause_wait:
    LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
    LD XDE, (FRAME_START_TICKS)
    SUB XWA, XDE            ; XWA = elapsed
    CP XWA, XBC
    JP ULT, _pause_wait     ; keep waiting if elapsed < target

    ; Frame completed on time
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA   ; store actual elapsed
    LDB (FRAME_OVERRAN), 0
    POP XIX
    RET

    RET

_end_overrun_indicator:
```

2. `make test` — run in MAME:

# Plan: Fix Polygon Rendering Glitches

## Context

The Another World VM port on KN5000 shows a grey screen with correct palette but **no visible polygon content**. After analyzing the polygon rendering pipeline against the reference MAME HLE implementation, three bugs were found that cause incorrect rendering and potential memory corruption.

**File to modify:** `src/another_world_vm.asm`

## Bug #1: drawLine off-by-one (causes buffer overflow/corruption)

**Location:** `drawLineN` (line 101), `drawLineP` (line 140), `drawLineBlend` (line 167)

**Problem:** Loop count `HL = xmax - xmin` is used with `DJNZ HL`, which decrements-then-tests. This draws `xmax - xmin` pixels instead of `xmax - xmin + 1` (inclusive range).

**Critical case:** When `xmax == xmin` (single pixel), `HL = 0`. DJNZ decrements to `0xFFFF` (non-zero), causing 65,536 iterations — massive buffer overflow that corrupts all VM state. This is likely the root cause of the rendering failure.

**Fix:** Add `INC HL` after `SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)` in all three functions:

- `drawLineN` line 101: `SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)` → add `INC HL` after
- `drawLineP` line 140: `SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)` → add `INC HL` after
- `drawLineBlend` line 167: `SUB HL, (LINE_XMIN)` → add `INC HL` after

## Bug #2: fillPolygon hliney > 199 jumps to wrong label

**Location:** `fillPolygon` line 716-717

**Problem:** When `HLINEY > 199`, the code jumps to `POLYGON_RASTER_LOOP` which continues processing the next polygon segment. The reference code does `return` (exits the entire fillPolygon function). This causes polygons that extend below the screen to continue rendering with wrong edge parameters, producing garbage.

**Current code:**
```asm
CPW (HLINEY), 199
JP GT, POLYGON_RASTER_LOOP    ; BUG: continues with next segment
```

**Fix:**
```asm
CPW (HLINEY), 199
JP GT, end_of_fillPolygon      ; EXIT: stop rendering this polygon
```

## Bug #3: drawPoint writes to wrong location and size

**Location:** `drawPoint` lines 181-192

**Problem (3 issues):**
1. Writes to hardcoded VRAM address `0x1A0000` instead of `CUR_PAGE_PTR_1` (page buffer)
2. `LD (XIX), BC` writes 2 bytes instead of 1 (writes color C + garbage B)
3. `LD WA, 0` doesn't clear upper XWA bits; subsequent `MUL XWA, 320` may use garbage upper bits (actually MUL XWA,DE does WA×DE→XWA so upper bits get overwritten — but XDE upper bits from `ADD XWA, XDE` are still garbage)

**Fix:** Replace with:
```asm
drawPoint:
    PUSH XIX
    LD XWA, 0
    LD WA, HL              ; XWA = y (zero-extended 32-bit)
    LD DE, 320
    MUL XWA, DE            ; XWA = y * 320
    EXTZ XDE               ; zero-extend x to 32-bit
    ADD XWA, XDE           ; XWA = y*320 + x
    LD XIX, (CUR_PAGE_PTR_1)
    ADD XIX, XWA
    LDB (XIX), C           ; write 1 byte (color)
    POP XIX
    RET
```

## Verification

1. `make clean && make` — must build without errors
2. `make test` — run in MAME, verify polygon content appears on screen after setPalette
3. The intro cinematic should show the Interplay logo and opening sequence polygons instead of a solid grey screen

# Plan: Timer-Based Frame Timing with Overrun Detection

## Context

The Another World intro plays slowly in some scenes. The current frame timing uses a fixed busy-wait loop (`PAUSE`) that ignores the VM's `variable[0xFF]` (pause slices), which specifies how many 20ms slices each frame should display. Additionally, there's no way to identify which frames exceed their time budget, making performance optimization blind.

**Goal:** Use TMP94C241F hardware timers for precise frame pacing, and add visible diagnostics for frame overruns.

## How AW Frame Timing Should Work (Reference)

The VM bytecode writes a value (typically 1-5) to variable `0xFF` specifying frame duration in 20ms slices:
- 1 slice = 20ms (50 Hz), 2 slices = 40ms (25 Hz), etc.

The reference implementation: `timeToSleep = var[0xFF] * 20ms - elapsedTime`. If elapsed > target, the frame overran (no sleep).

Currently, `PAUSE` is a fixed ~65K-iteration busy-loop called from `BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER` (opcode 0x10). It doesn't read var 0xFF and has no concept of elapsed time.

## Files to Modify

- `src/boot_hw_init.asm` — Add T0/T1 timer cascade initialization
- `src/main.asm` — Add INTT1 ISR, extend vector table, add RAM variables
- `src/another_world_vm.asm` — Rewrite PAUSE, record frame start time, add overrun indicator

## Step 1: Timer Hardware Setup (`src/boot_hw_init.asm`)

Add T0/T1 cascade timer initialization (same config as original KN5000 firmware). At the end of boot_hw_init.asm, before the implicit return:

```asm
; === 8-bit Timer Setup (T0/T1 cascade for system tick) ===
LD (T01MOD), 01dh       ; T0: T32 clock (fSYS/32), T1: cascade from T0
LD (T02FFCR), 000h      ; No flip-flop
LD (TREG0), 00ah        ; T0 divides by 10
LD (TREG1), 010h        ; T1 divides by 16
LD (TRDC), 000h         ; No double-buffer
SET 1, (T8RUN)          ; Start T0+T1

; Enable INTT1 interrupt at priority level 6
LD (INTET01), 0C0h      ; bits [7:5] = 110 = level 6, INTT0 disabled
```

**Tick rate at 25 MHz:** fSYS/32 = 781,250 Hz → ÷10 (T0) → ÷16 (T1) = **4,882.8 Hz** (~204.8 µs per tick).

**20ms = ~98 ticks.** Pre-computed constant: `TICKS_PER_SLICE EQU 98`

## Step 2: Interrupt Handler and Vector Table (`src/main.asm`)

**ISR** (minimal, placed before or after `Default_Handler`):

```asm
INTT1_Handler:
    PUSH XWA
    LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
    INC 1, XWA              ; 32-bit increment
    LD (SYSTEM_TICKS), XWA
    POP XWA
    RETI
```

**Extend vector table** from 8 entries to 22 (covers through offset 0x54 = INTT1):

```asm
ORG 0FFFF00h
VECTOR_TABLE:
    dd 00FFFEE0h           ; 0x00: Reset
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x04
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x08
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x0C
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x10
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x14
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x18
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x1C
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x20
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x24
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x28: INT0
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x2C: INT4
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x30: INT5
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x34: INT6
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x38: INT7
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x3C: reserved
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x40: INT8
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x44: INT9
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x48: INTA
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x4C: INTB
    dd Default_Handler     ; 0x50: INTT0
    dd INTT1_Handler       ; 0x54: INTT1 ← our timer ISR
```

**Add RAM variables** (after `CUR_VIDEO_DATA` in the RAM section):

```asm
SYSTEM_TICKS:        DD ?   ; 32-bit tick counter (ISR-incremented, ~4883 Hz)
FRAME_START_TICKS:   DD ?   ; Tick count at frame start
LAST_FRAME_TICKS:    DW ?   ; Elapsed ticks of last frame (for diagnostics)
FRAME_OVERRAN:       DB ?   ; 1 if last frame exceeded budget, 0 otherwise
```

## Step 3: Enable Interrupts (`src/another_world_vm.asm`)

Change `EI 06` (disables all maskable interrupts) to `EI 0` (accepts all priority levels):

```asm
ENTRY:
    EI 0    ; Enable interrupts (was EI 06 = disabled)
```

This is safe because only INTT1 has a non-zero priority (level 6). All other interrupt sources default to priority 0 (disabled) after reset.

## Step 4: Record Frame Start Time (`src/another_world_vm.asm`)

In `NEXT_THREAD`, at the end-of-frame boundary (after `CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS`, before `UPDATE_DISPLAY`), record the frame start time for the **next** frame:

```asm
; == END OF FRAME ==
LDB (CURRENT_THREAD), 0
CALL CHECK_THREAD_REQUESTS
LD A, 0FEh
CALL UPDATE_DISPLAY

; Record frame start time for next frame
LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
LD (FRAME_START_TICKS), XWA

LD A, 0
```

Also initialize `FRAME_START_TICKS` in `ENTRY` (before `MAIN_LOOP`):

```asm
LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
LD (FRAME_START_TICKS), XWA
```

## Step 5: Rewrite PAUSE (`src/another_world_vm.asm`)

Replace the fixed busy-loop with timer-based delay that reads VM variable 0xFF:

```asm
TICKS_PER_SLICE EQU 98     ; ~20ms at 4882.8 Hz tick rate

PAUSE:
    ; Read VM variable 0xFF (pause slices)
    PUSH XIX                ; save bytecode pointer
    LD A, 0FFh
    CALL _read_vm_var       ; DE = var[0xFF] (number of 20ms slices)

    ; Compute target ticks = slices * TICKS_PER_SLICE
    ; If slices == 0, use default of 1
    CP DE, 0
    JP NE, _pause_has_slices
    LD DE, 1
_pause_has_slices:
    LD WA, TICKS_PER_SLICE
    MUL XWA, DE             ; XWA = target_ticks (32-bit, but fits 16-bit)
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA  ; save target for reference (temporary, overwritten below)
    PUSH XWA                ; save target_ticks

    ; Compute elapsed = SYSTEM_TICKS - FRAME_START_TICKS
    LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
    LD XDE, (FRAME_START_TICKS)
    SUB XWA, XDE            ; XWA = elapsed ticks

    ; Check for overrun
    POP XDE                 ; XDE = target_ticks
    CP XWA, XDE
    JP UGE, _pause_overrun  ; elapsed >= target → overrun

    ; Wait for remaining time
    LD XBC, XDE             ; XBC = target_ticks
_pause_wait:
    LD XWA, (SYSTEM_TICKS)
    LD XDE, (FRAME_START_TICKS)
    SUB XWA, XDE            ; XWA = elapsed
    CP XWA, XBC
    JP ULT, _pause_wait     ; keep waiting if elapsed < target

    ; Frame completed on time
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA   ; store actual elapsed
    LDB (FRAME_OVERRAN), 0
    POP XIX
    RET

_pause_overrun:
    ; Frame took longer than budget
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA   ; store actual elapsed
    LDB (FRAME_OVERRAN), 1
    POP XIX
    RET
```

## Step 6: Overrun Visual Indicator (`src/another_world_vm.asm`)

After `CALL PAUSE` in `BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER`, add a simple visual indicator — write a colored pixel at the top-right corner of the VGA framebuffer. Red (color index depends on current palette) for overrun, black for on-time:

```asm
; After CALL PAUSE in BLIT_FRAMEBUFFER:
LD A, (FRAME_OVERRAN)
CP A, 0
JP EQ, _no_overrun_indicator
; Overrun: write bright pixel at (319, 0)
LDB (001a0000h + 20*320 + 319), 0Fh   ; color 15 (white in most palettes)
JP _end_overrun_indicator
_no_overrun_indicator:
LDB (001a0000h + 20*320 + 319), 00h   ; color 0 (background)
_end_overrun_indicator:
```

This writes directly to VRAM at the top-right pixel after the blit, so it's visible on screen without affecting the page buffers.

## Verification

1. `make clean && make` — must build without errors
2. `make test` — run in MAME:
   - Verify the intro still plays correctly (timer didn't break anything)
   - Check if frame pacing feels more natural (scenes that were too slow should now use var 0xFF timing)
   - Look for white pixel flashes at top-right corner indicating frame overruns
3. In MAME debugger: examine `SYSTEM_TICKS` to verify timer is incrementing, `LAST_FRAME_TICKS` for frame durations, `FRAME_OVERRAN` for overrun detection

    JP ULT, _pause_wait     ; keep waiting if elapsed < target

    ; Frame completed on time
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA   ; store actual elapsed
    LDB (FRAME_OVERRAN), 0
    POP XIX
    RET

_pause_overrun:
    ; Frame took longer than budget
    LD (LAST_FRAME_TICKS), WA   ; store actual elapsed
    LDB (FRAME_OVERRAN), 1
    POP XIX
    RET
```
